title: AI ambition aligned to organisational strategy
objective: The organisation has a stated ambition for AI that is derived from its own strategy and objectives, and that leaders and staff can describe.
level_1: No stated ambition; AI activity is driven by individual interest or supplier offers.
level_2: An ambition or vision statement exists, but it is generic, not linked to organisational objectives, or not agreed by leadership.
level_3: An approved AI ambition, owned by a named person and expressed in terms of the organisation's objectives, is known across the organisation.
level_4: Progress against the ambition is measured and reported, and AI activity that does not serve it is identified and challenged.
level_5: The ambition is refined from evidence of what AI has delivered and from changes in the organisation's strategy.

title: Where AI will and will not be used
objective: The organisation has decided, and recorded with reasons, the areas of its work where AI is encouraged, where it is allowed only under conditions, and where it is ruled out.
level_1: No stated boundaries; whether AI is suitable for an area is argued case by case, if at all.
level_2: Some areas are informally favoured or avoided, but this is not written down, not reasoned, or not agreed by leadership.
level_3: Approved strategic boundaries say where AI is encouraged, conditional or ruled out and why, fit the risk appetite and the policy, and keep some decisions with people.
level_4: Proposals and live uses are checked against the boundaries, and pressure on them (repeated requests in a ruled-out area, for example) is reported and considered.
level_5: Boundaries are adjusted from evidence such as outcomes, incidents and external change, and the reasons for each change are published internally.

title: Investment and funding for AI
objective: The organisation has a defined approach to funding AI, covering what is paid for centrally and locally, how long commitments last, and how requests for money are judged.
level_1: AI is funded from whatever local budgets teams can find; there is no view of total spend.
level_2: Some central or ring-fenced funding exists, but the rules for accessing it are unclear, it is year to year only, or it covers pilots and not running costs.
level_3: A documented approach to funding AI sets central and local responsibilities, longer commitments where needed and published criteria, and is followed across the organisation.
level_4: Total AI spend is known and reported against the funding approach, and funded work is reviewed against what it was funded to deliver.
level_5: Funding allocation is adjusted from evidence of which investments delivered value, and the approach is refined each planning cycle.

title: Organisation-level value case
objective: The organisation has stated the value it expects from AI across its work, by type of value, with the assumptions behind each estimate written down.
level_1: No organisation-level view of expected value; benefits are claimed use by use, if at all.
level_2: Expected value is described in general terms, without estimates, assumptions or a split by type of value.
level_3: An approved, owned value case states the gains expected from AI and the assumptions behind them, and is used in strategy and funding decisions.
level_4: The value case is compared with tracked benefits from live uses, and assumptions that prove wrong are reported and corrected.
level_5: The value case is refined each cycle from measured outcomes, and its accuracy over time is itself tracked.

title: Horizon scanning and external expectations
objective: The organisation tracks changes in AI technology, regulation, peer practice and public expectation, and feeds what it finds into its AI strategy.
level_1: No organised scanning; individuals follow developments informally and share them ad hoc.
level_2: Some scanning happens, for example a newsletter or occasional briefing, but it is not linked to strategy decisions.
level_3: An owned horizon scanning activity covers technology, regulation, peers and public expectation, produces regular output and informs strategy decisions.
level_4: Findings are logged with the action taken on each, and the time from a relevant external change to a strategy response is tracked.
level_5: Scanning anticipates change well enough that the organisation acts ahead of it, and the scanning sources and method are reviewed against how useful they proved.

title: Multi-year AI roadmap tied to planning
objective: The organisation has a phased AI roadmap that is linked to its business and financial planning cycles and shows the points where it will decide whether to proceed.
level_1: No roadmap; AI work is planned project by project, if at all.
level_2: A roadmap exists but is a list of projects, is not linked to business or financial planning, or has no decision points.
level_3: An approved, owned multi-year roadmap follows the planning cycles, sets decision points with criteria and names the capacity planned uses depend on.
level_4: Progress against the roadmap is reported, decisions at each point are recorded with their evidence, and slippage is acted on.
level_5: The roadmap is revised each planning cycle from delivery evidence, value achieved and external change.

title: Stakeholder input to strategy
objective: Staff, their representatives, service users, partners and, where relevant, the public and regulators have a real opportunity to shape the AI strategy, and the organisation can show what changed as a result.
level_1: The strategy is written by a small group without wider input.
level_2: Some groups are consulted, but late, selectively, or with no record of what they said or what changed.
level_3: A planned engagement approach involves the relevant stakeholder groups before the strategy is settled and records what they said and how the organisation responded.
level_4: The reach and influence of engagement are measured, gaps in who has been heard are identified, and stakeholders are told what changed because of them.
level_5: Stakeholder involvement is a continuing part of how the strategy is developed, and the approach is improved from participants' feedback.

title: Strategy review cycle
objective: The AI strategy is reviewed on a set cycle and whenever defined triggers occur, and each change is recorded with its reason.
level_1: The strategy is not reviewed once written, or is rewritten only when leadership changes.
level_2: Reviews happen, but irregularly, without defined triggers, or without a record of what changed and why.
level_3: The AI strategy is reviewed by its owner on a set cycle and when defined triggers occur, and each change is recorded with its reason.
level_4: Reviews draw on measured evidence such as value achieved, risk and incident trends and horizon scanning, and actions from each review are tracked to completion.
level_5: The review cycle and triggers are themselves adjusted from experience, so the strategy is updated at the pace the organisation needs.

title: AI policy
objective: The organisation has an approved AI policy that states which uses of AI are permitted, which need approval and which are not allowed, and keeps it current.
level_1: No organisation-wide policy; individual teams or staff set their own rules.
level_2: A policy or guidance note exists but is incomplete, unapproved, or not widely known.
level_3: An approved, owned and controlled AI policy sets the scope of AI governance and which uses are permitted, need approval or are prohibited, and all staff know it.
level_4: Policy awareness and compliance are measured; the policy is reviewed on schedule and after significant incidents or external change.
level_5: The policy is refined from evidence of how AI is actually used, incidents and lessons, and stays ahead of external change rather than reacting to it.

title: Executive accountability
objective: A named senior executive is accountable for the organisation's use of AI, with a defined remit, and reports on it to the board or equivalent.
level_1: No one is accountable; AI is treated as a technology matter or left to enthusiasts.
level_2: Someone is informally seen as the lead, but the remit is unclear or lacks authority.
level_3: A named senior executive is formally accountable for AI under a written remit and reports on AI to the board or equivalent as a standing item.
level_4: The board receives regular, evidence-based reporting on AI benefits, risks and performance, and challenges it.
level_5: Accountability arrangements are reviewed against outcomes and adjusted as AI use grows or changes in nature.

title: Decision rights proportionate to risk
objective: Decision rights for approving, changing and retiring uses of AI are defined, scaled to risk, and followed.
level_1: No defined approval route; uses of AI start wherever someone decides to try them.
level_2: An approval route exists for some uses or some parts of the organisation, or is the same for all uses regardless of risk.
level_3: Risk-tiered decision rights for approving, changing and retiring uses of AI are applied everywhere, screen out prohibited practices and stop uses beyond the risk appetite.
level_4: Decisions are recorded and periodically checked against the tiers; bypasses are detected and dealt with.
level_5: Tiers and thresholds are adjusted from evidence such as time to decision, incidents and outcomes, so the route stays proportionate.

title: Oversight forum
objective: A cross-functional forum oversees AI use, risk and performance, with terms of reference, the right membership and a clear link to the organisation's main governance.
level_1: No forum; AI matters surface ad hoc in other meetings, if at all.
level_2: An informal group or community of interest meets, but it has no remit to decide or escalate.
level_3: A diverse, cross-functional oversight forum works to terms of reference, meets on a set cycle, records its decisions and can escalate.
level_4: The forum tracks its decisions to completion and reports measured performance, risk and benefit to the accountable executive.
level_5: The forum's remit, membership and cadence are reviewed against its effect and adjusted as AI use matures.

title: Named owners for each use of AI
objective: Every use of AI has named owners for the business outcome, the data, the technology and its assurance, recorded where others can find them.
level_1: Ownership is assumed rather than assigned; often only the person who set it up knows.
level_2: Some uses have a named owner, usually technical, but business and data ownership are gaps.
level_3: Every use of AI has named business, data, technical and assurance owners in the inventory, and ownership changes hands formally with residual risk accepted.
level_4: Ownership is checked when people move roles, and gaps are caught and filled within a set time.
level_5: Owners actively manage their uses against measures, and ownership arrangements are improved from experience.

title: AI inventory
objective: The organisation keeps a current inventory of the AI it uses, including AI built into bought products and services, with enough detail to govern it.
level_1: No inventory; knowledge of what AI is in use is scattered or absent.
level_2: A partial list exists, usually of in-house projects, missing AI embedded in bought products or used informally.
level_3: A maintained inventory covers in-house, procured and embedded AI, with the details needed to govern each entry and links to its models, data and integrations.
level_4: The inventory is reconciled against procurement, technology and data records, and its completeness is measured.
level_5: The inventory feeds portfolio, risk and transparency reporting automatically and is used as the organisation's single view of AI.

title: Integration with existing governance
objective: AI governance works through the organisation's existing risk, information, data protection, security and procurement governance rather than alongside it.
level_1: AI is handled entirely outside existing governance, or ignored by it.
level_2: Some links exist, for example data protection reviews AI cases, but the routes are informal and inconsistent.
level_3: Existing governance processes each have a defined AI step that the AI route calls on, with information and data protection advice involved from the start.
level_4: Hand-offs between AI and existing governance are tracked, and duplication or gaps are identified and closed.
level_5: AI considerations are part of how existing governance normally works, and no separate track is needed for routine decisions.

title: Policy compliance and exceptions
objective: Compliance with the AI policy is monitored, and exceptions are requested, approved, recorded and reviewed.
level_1: Compliance is not checked; exceptions happen informally or unseen.
level_2: Compliance is checked occasionally or after problems; exceptions are agreed verbally or by email without a record.
level_3: Compliance with the AI policy is checked on a defined basis, and exceptions go through a recorded process with approval, expiry, risk and treatment.
level_4: Compliance results and exception trends are reported to the oversight forum, and repeat exceptions trigger policy review.
level_5: Monitoring is largely built into tools and processes, and exception data routinely improves the policy.

title: Public transparency about AI use
objective: The organisation publishes information about how and why it uses AI, to the extent its obligations and public role require, and keeps it current.
level_1: No public information about AI use.
level_2: Some information is published, for example a statement or a single record, but it is incomplete or out of date.
level_3: Decisions on what to publish about each use of AI are recorded, required records and registrations are completed and kept current, and sensitive communications are cleared.
level_4: Publication is checked against the AI inventory for completeness, and public questions and feedback are tracked and answered.
level_5: Transparency is used as a design input: uses of AI are shaped so they can be explained publicly from the start.

title: Review and disclosure of AI-generated content
objective: The organisation has approved rules for reviewing and disclosing AI-generated content that it releases or relies on, so people know when AI was used.
level_1: Whether AI-generated content is reviewed or disclosed is left to the person who produced it.
level_2: Some teams review or label AI-generated content, but the rules are incomplete, unapproved or not widely known, or content used inside the organisation is not covered.
level_3: Approved rules set how AI-generated content released outside the organisation, or used inside it for decisions and official records, is reviewed and disclosed, clearly and at least as the law requires.
level_4: Compliance with the review and disclosure rules is measured, and the rules are reviewed on schedule and after significant incidents or legal change.
level_5: The rules are refined from evidence of how AI-generated content is actually used and received, and stay ahead of external change rather than reacting to it.

title: AI risk appetite
objective: The board or equivalent has approved a statement of how much AI risk the organisation will accept, broken down by kind of risk, and it is used in decisions.
level_1: No statement of AI risk appetite; tolerance depends on whoever is deciding.
level_2: AI is mentioned in the general risk appetite, or a draft AI statement exists, but it does not distinguish kinds of risk or is not approved.
level_3: A board-approved, owned AI risk appetite sets tolerances by kind of risk, has a review date and is referred to in approval decisions.
level_4: Exposure across live and proposed uses is reported against the appetite, and decisions that exceed it are escalated and recorded.
level_5: The appetite is recalibrated from evidence of outcomes, incidents and external change, and the board reviews whether it is enabling the intended use of AI.

title: AI risk assessment method
objective: The organisation uses one consistent, documented method to assess the risks of each use of AI, and the results feed its corporate risk management.
level_1: AI risk is assessed, if at all, by individual judgement with no common method.
level_2: A method or checklist exists, but it is used in some areas only, does not cover risks particular to AI, or sits outside corporate risk management.
level_3: A documented, proportionate method assesses every use of AI before approval and in live use, records treatment and residual risk, and feeds corporate risk registers.
level_4: Assessments are quality checked, and the AI risk profile, including trends in residual risk, is reported to the oversight forum.
level_5: The method is refined from incidents, near misses and assessment reviews, and its results are shown to predict where problems occur.

title: Impact assessment before deployment
objective: Before a use of AI goes live, its likely effects on people and groups (including equality, privacy, rights and safety) and on society and the environment are assessed to a depth that matches its risk, and the findings are acted on.
level_1: Effects on people are not assessed before go-live, or only after a complaint.
level_2: Some impact assessment happens, for example for data protection, but equality, rights and safety are not covered consistently, or findings are not acted on.
level_3: A proportionate impact assessment covering people, workforce, society and environment is signed off before each in-scope use goes live, kept current, and its mitigations tracked.
level_4: Completion and quality of impact assessments are checked, assessments are revisited after significant change, and actual effects in live use are compared with what was predicted.
level_5: Impact assessment shapes design from the start, and the method is improved from evidence of effects it missed.

title: Legal and regulatory obligations
objective: The organisation keeps a current view of the laws, regulations and standards that apply to its use of AI, with an owner for each obligation and a way of checking it is met.
level_1: No view of which obligations apply to AI use; legal advice is sought only when a problem arises.
level_2: Some obligations are known and tracked, typically data protection, but the view is incomplete, unowned or out of date.
level_3: An owned, reviewed register of AI obligations guides design and approval, and each use records its regulatory role, duties, regulator contact and how obligations are shared.
level_4: Compliance with each obligation is checked and reported, and new or changed obligations are assessed for effect within a set time.
level_5: The organisation anticipates regulatory change, shapes its practice ahead of it, and contributes to consultations where it has relevant experience.

title: Ethical principles in practice
objective: The organisation has adopted ethical principles for AI and applies them through a working review route that can change or stop a use of AI.
level_1: No adopted principles; ethical questions are left to individuals.
level_2: Principles are published, but there is no route for applying them to real cases, or the route is advisory and rarely used.
level_3: Adopted ethical principles are applied through a working review route with triggers and authority, used at the outset of each use and for recorded trade-offs.
level_4: Review outcomes are tracked to completion, the route's use and effect are reported, and cases that should have been reviewed but were not are identified.
level_5: Principles and the review route are refined from case experience and stakeholder feedback, and reasoning from past cases is reused as guidance.

title: Fairness and bias management
objective: Unfair bias is identified, tested for and reduced at each stage of a use of AI, from design through to live operation.
level_1: Bias is not considered, or is assumed not to be present.
level_2: Bias is considered for some uses, usually at design, but testing is informal and live use is not checked.
level_3: A documented fairness approach defines groups and measures for each in-scope use, tests before release, records mitigations and proxies, and monitors fairness in live use.
level_4: Fairness breaches in live use lead to investigation, root-cause analysis and action, and fairness results are reported to the oversight forum.
level_5: Fairness methods are improved from monitoring results and external developments, and lessons are shared across uses.

title: Human oversight proportionate to risk
objective: Each use of AI has human oversight designed to match its risk, stating who reviews, at which point, and with what authority to override or stop it.
level_1: Oversight is not designed; whether anyone checks AI outputs depends on the individual.
level_2: Some uses have a human review step, but its purpose, timing and authority are not defined, or reviewers lack the information to challenge outputs.
level_3: Every use of AI has a documented, risk-based oversight model with trained reviewers, tested before go-live to show they can detect problems and intervene.
level_4: Oversight is checked in practice, for example override rates and review times, and signs of rubber-stamping or overload are acted on.
level_5: Oversight designs are refined from evidence of where human review adds value and where it does not.

title: Explanation and challenge for affected people
objective: People affected by decisions that AI supports can find out that AI was involved, get an explanation they can understand, and challenge the outcome through a route that can change it.
level_1: Affected people are not told AI was involved and have no specific route to question the outcome.
level_2: Explanations or challenge are available for some uses, or on request only, and the route may not be able to change outcomes.
level_3: People know when AI is involved in decisions about them or in their interactions, can get a meaningful explanation, and can challenge outcomes through human review.
level_4: Requests for explanation and challenges are logged, outcomes and response times are measured, and patterns are fed back to the owners of the use.
level_5: Explanation and challenge are designed in from the start, and the route is improved from the experience of the people who use it.

title: Risk of AI from suppliers
objective: Before AI in a bought product or service is used, and when it changes, the organisation assesses what it does, how it uses data, how the supplier changes the model, and what assurance the supplier offers.
level_1: AI in bought products is not identified or assessed; it is accepted as part of the product.
level_2: Some suppliers are asked about AI, but questions are ad hoc, cover only new purchases, or miss updates that add AI to existing products.
level_3: Standard due diligence covers AI in new and existing bought products before use and at intervals, feeds each risk assessment, and keeps unregistered high-risk AI out.
level_4: Gaps in supplier assurance are tracked to closure and reported, and reassessment results inform renewal and purchasing decisions.
level_5: Due diligence is refined from incidents and supplier experience, and the organisation's requirements shape what suppliers offer.

title: Idea intake open to all staff
objective: Anyone in the organisation can propose a use of AI through a simple, well-known route, and every proposal is acknowledged and considered.
level_1: No route for proposals; ideas progress only if someone senior or technical takes them up.
level_2: A route exists in some teams or functions, or is not widely known, and proposals are not always answered.
level_3: A single, documented and owned intake route is open to all staff and publicised, and every proposal is acknowledged and logged in the pipeline register.
level_4: Volumes, sources and response times are measured, and parts of the organisation that submit little are followed up.
level_5: The intake route is refined from proposer feedback and conversion rates, and actively draws in ideas from under-represented groups and functions.

title: Agreed prioritisation criteria
objective: Proposed uses of AI are ranked against published criteria covering value, feasibility, risk, cost and strategic fit, applied the same way to every proposal.
level_1: Proposals are chosen by preference, enthusiasm or who is asking.
level_2: Criteria exist but are informal, unpublished, or applied differently by different teams.
level_3: Approved, published criteria covering value, feasibility, risk, cost and strategic fit are applied to every proposal, with scoring and decisions recorded.
level_4: Consistency of scoring is checked, and the realised value and cost of chosen uses are compared with their scores to test the criteria.
level_5: Criteria and weightings are adjusted from portfolio outcomes and changes in strategy, and the effect of each change is reviewed.

title: Pipeline register of proposed uses
objective: A single register records every proposed and in-flight use of AI with its status, owner and decision history, and hands each entry to the AI inventory when it goes live.
level_1: No register; proposed and in-flight work is known only to the people doing it.
level_2: Lists are kept by individual teams or for some uses, with inconsistent fields and no decision history.
level_3: A single maintained register records every proposed and in-flight use with its status, owner, stage and decisions, and hands live uses to the inventory.
level_4: Register completeness and accuracy are checked, stalled entries are flagged and resolved, and register data is reported to the oversight forum.
level_5: The register is used to manage the portfolio as a whole, informing capacity, funding and reuse decisions, and its design is improved from use.

title: Stage gates from idea to retirement
objective: Each use of AI passes through defined stages (explore, pilot, scale, operate, retire), with entry and exit criteria checked at each gate.
level_1: No defined stages; work moves forward by default until someone stops it.
level_2: Stages are described but criteria are vague or optional, or gates are used only for some uses.
level_3: Documented, risk-proportionate stages with entry and exit criteria apply to every use, with gate decisions and a running design record kept.
level_4: Gate outcomes and time spent at each stage are measured, and uses that skip or stall at a gate are identified and dealt with.
level_5: Gate criteria and stages are refined from evidence of which checks catch problems and which only add delay.

title: Proportionate business case
objective: Each use of AI has a business case scaled to its size and risk that states expected benefits, full costs and assumptions, and is approved before significant commitment.
level_1: Uses go ahead without a stated case; benefits are assumed rather than described.
level_2: Business cases are written for some uses, often large ones, but costs or benefits are incomplete or not quantified.
level_3: Every use of AI has a plain-language business case, scaled by a template to its size and risk, covering problem, benefits, costs, assumptions and options, approved at a gate.
level_4: Business case assumptions are revisited at later gates, and cases that no longer hold lead to a recorded decision to continue, change or stop.
level_5: Estimates are calibrated against actual costs and benefits from past uses, so cases become more accurate over time.

title: Safe experimentation
objective: Staff can try AI quickly within defined guardrails covering approved environments, data limits, time limits and exit criteria.
level_1: No sanctioned route to experiment; trials happen informally, often with unapproved tools or real data.
level_2: Some teams have a place or permission to experiment, but rules on data, duration and exit are unclear or inconsistent.
level_3: A documented experimentation route with approved environments, data rules, time limits and exit criteria is open to all teams and used.
level_4: Experiments are logged and checked against the guardrails, breaches are acted on, and the route's speed and take-up are measured.
level_5: Guardrails and environments are adjusted from what experiments reveal, so the route stays fast and safe as tools and needs change.

title: Pilot to production decisions
objective: Every pilot ends in a recorded decision to scale, extend or stop, made against criteria and evidence agreed before the pilot started.
level_1: Pilots continue or end by default; decisions are not recorded.
level_2: Some pilots have success criteria, but they are set late, loosely defined, or not used to decide.
level_3: Every pilot has success and stop criteria agreed at the start and ends in a recorded, evidence-based decision to scale, extend or stop.
level_4: Pilot outcomes are tracked across the portfolio, extensions are time-limited and reviewed, and pilots running past their end date are flagged and resolved.
level_5: Decision criteria and pilot design are improved from how scaled uses perform in live service.

title: Reuse across the organisation
objective: Successful patterns, components and lessons from uses of AI are recorded so others can find them, and are reused before anything new is built.
level_1: Each team starts from scratch; reuse happens only through personal contacts.
level_2: Some patterns or components are shared, but there is no place to find them and no expectation to look.
level_3: Reusable patterns, components and lessons are recorded in a known place, checked before new work starts, and each shared component has an owner.
level_4: The amount of reuse and the effort it saves are measured, and proposals that duplicate existing work are caught at intake or the first gate.
level_5: Assets are designed for reuse from the start, and the reuse library is curated and improved from how it is used.

title: Retiring uses of AI
objective: Uses of AI that no longer earn their place are withdrawn through a planned process that covers users, dependent processes and disposal or retention of models and data.
level_1: Uses are left running or switched off without a plan; models and data are left in place.
level_2: Some uses are retired deliberately, but steps for users, data and models are worked out each time.
level_3: A documented retirement process, triggered by periodic review, withdraws uses of AI with care for users, people, data, models and hardware, and updates the inventory.
level_4: Live uses are routinely reviewed against retirement triggers, retirements are checked for completion, and leftover models or data are found and dealt with.
level_5: Retirement is planned from the design stage, and the process is refined from lessons of past withdrawals.

title: Target operating model for AI
objective: The organisation has a defined, approved operating model that states who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, and what is done centrally and what locally.
level_1: No defined model; AI work is done wherever capability and interest happen to exist.
level_2: A model is described or emerging, but responsibilities between central and local teams are unclear or not followed.
level_3: An approved operating model sets out who builds, buys, runs and supports AI, centrally and locally, through named and resourced teams, and is followed across the organisation.
level_4: The model's performance is measured, for example delivery times, capacity and demand, and work done outside it is identified and addressed.
level_5: The model is reviewed against outcomes and adjusted as AI use grows or its nature changes.

title: Build, buy or configure approach
objective: A consistent, documented method decides for each use of AI whether to configure tools already owned, procure, build, or wait, and the reasons are recorded.
level_1: Sourcing choices are made case by case, usually by whoever starts the work.
level_2: Some guidance exists, but it is not used consistently or does not consider configuring existing tools or waiting.
level_3: A documented sourcing method with set criteria decides whether to configure, procure, build or wait for every use of AI, and each decision is recorded.
level_4: Sourcing decisions are reviewed against actual cost, delivery time and supportability, and departures from the method are explained and approved.
level_5: The method's criteria are updated from the outcomes of past decisions and changes in the market.

title: Running cost management
objective: The ongoing cost of each AI service, including usage-based charges, is known, forecast, assigned to an owner and kept within agreed limits.
level_1: Running costs are not tracked separately; they surface in general budgets after the event.
level_2: Costs are tracked for some services, but forecasts, usage limits or cost owners are missing.
level_3: Running costs of every AI service are tracked, forecast and held by a budget holder, with usage limits or alerts and regular review against budget.
level_4: Cost per unit of use is measured and compared with the business case, overspends trigger action, and unused licences or capacity are removed.
level_5: Cost data shapes design and sourcing choices, and pricing models are renegotiated or changed from evidence of how services are used.

title: AI-aware procurement and contracts
objective: Contracts for AI products and services set clear terms on data rights, intellectual property, notice of model changes, transparency and exit.
level_1: AI is bought on standard terms with no AI-specific clauses.
level_2: AI-specific terms are added for some contracts, depending on who runs the procurement.
level_3: Standard AI contract terms, informed by the supplier risk assessment, are used in every relevant procurement and cover rights, change, transparency, security, assurance, resilience, exit and liability.
level_4: Contracts are checked for the standard terms before signature, departures are approved and recorded, and existing contracts are reviewed when renewed.
level_5: Standard terms are updated from supplier disputes, incidents, market practice and legal change.

title: Supplier performance and exit
objective: AI suppliers are managed against agreed performance measures, and each critical AI service has a tested route to exit or replace the supplier.
level_1: Suppliers are not actively managed once the contract is signed; there is no exit plan.
level_2: Some suppliers are reviewed, but measures are informal and exit plans are missing or untested.
level_3: Every AI supplier has an owner and agreed performance measures reviewed regularly, and each critical AI service has a documented exit plan.
level_4: Supplier performance is reported and acted on, and exit plans for critical services are tested or rehearsed.
level_5: Supplier management and exit planning are refined from experience of supplier changes and exits.

title: Delivery standards for AI
objective: AI work is delivered by multidisciplinary teams using user-centred methods to defined delivery standards.
level_1: AI work is done by technical staff alone, with little contact with users.
level_2: Some projects use multidisciplinary teams or user research, but there is no common standard.
level_3: Documented delivery standards for multidisciplinary, user-centred AI delivery, with safety, security, privacy, accessibility and quality built in from design, are applied to all AI delivery.
level_4: Delivery is checked against the standards at gates, and user adoption and satisfaction are measured and acted on.
level_5: Delivery standards are improved from user outcomes and lessons across the portfolio.

title: Service management for live AI
objective: Every live AI service has defined support, change and problem management arrangements, including handling of changes to models and prompts.
level_1: Live AI is supported informally by whoever built it.
level_2: Some services are in the support process, but AI-specific changes such as model or prompt updates are not covered.
level_3: Every live AI service has a support owner, a problem reporting route for users, and change and problem management that covers AI-specific changes.
level_4: Service levels, problems and changes are measured and reported, and repeat problems lead to root cause fixes.
level_5: Service management practice for AI is refined from incident and change data and from user feedback.

title: Collaboration and sharing
objective: The organisation works with peer organisations and partners to share AI solutions, lessons and capacity where this serves its aims.
level_1: No deliberate collaboration; contact with peers happens through individuals.
level_2: Some collaboration or sharing takes place, but it is opportunistic and not tracked.
level_3: A stated approach guides collaboration with peers and partners, and solutions and lessons are shared and taken up under agreed data, intellectual property and ethical terms.
level_4: The value of collaboration is assessed, for example time or cost saved, and partnerships that do not deliver are changed or ended.
level_5: Collaboration shapes the organisation's AI plans, and it contributes to and learns from shared work as a matter of course.

title: Continuity when AI fails
objective: Services that depend on AI can continue safely when the AI is unavailable, degraded or producing wrong results, through planned fallbacks that have been tested.
level_1: Dependence on AI is not considered in continuity planning; a failure would be handled when it happened.
level_2: Some services have fallbacks, but they are informal, untested or do not cover degraded or wrong output.
level_3: Every service that depends on AI has a tested fallback or safe stop, based on an impact analysis and part of continuity plans, and people are told when it is used.
level_4: Recovery times are measured against targets, and failures in testing are fixed.
level_5: Continuity is improved from tests, incidents and supplier changes, and the degree of dependence on AI is set deliberately for each service.

title: Involving people in AI design and evaluation
objective: Evaluations and research that involve people have their informed consent, ethics review and protection, use participants who represent those the service will serve, and for significant uses draw on the communities affected.
level_1: Research and evaluation with people happen informally, without consent records or ethics review.
level_2: Some projects obtain consent or ethics review, but there is no common standard, participants are chosen for convenience, or affected communities are not engaged.
level_3: Evaluations and research involving people have informed consent, ethics review, representative participants and protection of wellbeing and the right to withdraw, and significant uses engage affected communities at planning and design.
level_4: Consent, ethics review and participant representation are checked at delivery gates, and community input and the response to it are reviewed for significant uses.
level_5: Research practice and community engagement are improved from participant feedback, outcomes and lessons across the portfolio.

title: Data strategy supports AI
objective: The organisation's data strategy states what its planned uses of AI need from data and sets out how those needs will be met.
level_1: No data strategy, or one that does not mention AI; data needs are discovered project by project.
level_2: The data strategy mentions AI in general terms, but does not state what data AI needs or how gaps will be closed.
level_3: An approved, owned data strategy sets out what planned AI needs from data and the actions and funding to meet it, backed by an approved data architecture.
level_4: Progress against the data actions that AI depends on is measured and reported, and slippage that puts AI plans at risk is escalated.
level_5: The data strategy and the AI strategy are revised together, using evidence of which data constraints have most limited AI value.

title: Data ownership and stewardship
objective: Every data set used by AI has a named accountable owner and day-to-day stewards who understand the data and look after it.
level_1: Ownership of data is unclear; system administrators or project teams make decisions about data by default.
level_2: Some important data sets have named owners, but stewardship is informal and data used by AI is not consistently covered.
level_3: Every data set used by AI has a named owner and steward, recorded centrally, with defined responsibilities for approving use, quality and access.
level_4: Coverage of ownership and stewardship is measured, gaps are filled within a set time, and owners are held to their responsibilities through regular review.
level_5: Owners and stewards actively shape how their data is used for AI, and the arrangements are improved from experience of where decisions were slow or missed.

title: Data quality fit for purpose
objective: The quality of data used by each AI system is assessed against what that use needs, and shortfalls are fixed or their effects managed before and during live use.
level_1: Data quality is assumed; problems are found when outputs look wrong.
level_2: Quality is checked for some uses or some data sets, without agreed measures or a link to what the AI use needs.
level_3: Quality requirements are set for each use of AI, data is assessed against them before and during use, and shortfalls are owned and remediated or mitigated.
level_4: Quality measures are tracked over time for data used by AI, falls below threshold trigger action, and the effect of quality on AI outputs is understood.
level_5: Quality issues are fixed at source, and requirements and checks are refined from evidence of which quality problems most affected AI outcomes.

title: Finding and understanding data
objective: Data available for AI is catalogued and described well enough that people can find it, understand what it means and its limits, and use it correctly.
level_1: Knowledge of what data exists sits with individuals; finding data means asking around.
level_2: Some data sets are listed or documented, but descriptions are incomplete, out of date or held in separate places.
level_3: A maintained catalogue describes data used or available for AI, including its owner, meaning, limits, conditions of use and sensitivity.
level_4: Catalogue completeness and accuracy are measured, and use of the catalogue is tracked to show whether people find what they need.
level_5: Catalogue entries are kept current largely as a by-product of normal data work, and descriptions are improved from feedback by the people using them.

title: Lawful and fair use of data
objective: Before data is used in an AI system, its use is confirmed as lawful, consistent with the purpose for which it was collected, and fair to the people it describes.
level_1: Data is used for AI wherever it is available; lawful basis and fairness are not considered.
level_2: Data protection advice is sought for some uses, usually late or only for obviously personal data.
level_3: Each use of data in AI has a lawful basis, purpose check and fairness consideration signed off before use, with data minimised and privacy techniques considered.
level_4: These records are checked for completeness against the AI inventory, are revisited when the use or the data changes, and gaps are acted on.
level_5: Lawful and fair use is designed in from the start of each use of AI, and the approach is refined from case outcomes, complaints and changes in law.

title: Records management for AI
objective: Retention and records rules cover what AI systems take in and produce, including prompts, outputs and the decisions they supported, and are applied in practice.
level_1: No one has considered whether AI inputs and outputs are records; retention depends on product defaults.
level_2: Some rules exist for some AI systems, but prompts, outputs and AI-supported decisions are not consistently covered.
level_3: Records and retention rules cover AI inputs, prompts, outputs, supported decisions and system logs, and are applied to every use of AI.
level_4: Application of the rules is checked, including retention settings in bought tools, and failures such as unretrievable records or late deletion are caught and fixed.
level_5: Records handling for AI is largely automated, and the rules are refined from requests for information, audits and changes in how AI is used.

title: Controlled access and sharing
objective: AI systems and their users can reach only the data they need for the agreed purpose, and data is shared into and out of AI systems only under agreed rules.
level_1: AI systems are given whatever access makes them work; sharing happens without agreed rules.
level_2: Access is restricted for some systems or data, but AI systems' own access is not reviewed and sharing rules are informal.
level_3: Access to data by AI systems and users is limited to the agreed purpose and approved, sharing follows agreements, and live sensitive data in development is controlled.
level_4: Access rights and sharing agreements for AI are reviewed on a set cycle, excess access is removed, and breaches of sharing rules are detected and acted on.
level_5: Access and sharing controls for AI are applied automatically from data classification and purpose, and are refined from review findings.

title: Provenance of training and test data
objective: For data used to train, tune or test AI, the organisation knows and records where it came from, what rights it holds over it, and any limits on its use.
level_1: Training and test data are gathered from wherever is convenient, and their origin is not recorded.
level_2: Origin is recorded for some data sets, but rights, licences and limits are not consistently checked.
level_3: For every data set used to train, tune or test AI, origin, rights, limits and preparation are recorded before use and linked to the models that used it.
level_4: Provenance records are checked for completeness before release, and when a source's rights or limits change, affected models are identified and acted on.
level_5: Provenance is captured automatically through data pipelines, and the approach is refined from audits, disputes and changes in rights or regulation.

title: Approved AI tools and platforms
objective: The organisation keeps a current list of approved AI tools and platforms, each with clear conditions of use, and staff know where to find it.
level_1: No approved list; staff choose tools themselves or wait for case-by-case answers.
level_2: Some tools are known to be allowed, but there is no maintained list, or conditions of use are missing or unclear.
level_3: A maintained, published list of approved AI tools and platforms states each one's permitted uses, data limits and owner, with a route to request additions.
level_4: The list is reviewed on a set cycle, requests are handled within an agreed time, and use of approved tools is measured against the conditions.
level_5: The list is refined from usage, requests and supplier change, and approval of new tools is quick enough that staff rarely look elsewhere.

title: Reference architecture for AI
objective: Agreed architecture patterns set out how AI components fit into the technology estate, and new uses of AI follow them or record why not.
level_1: No agreed patterns; each use of AI is designed from scratch.
level_2: Some patterns or preferred approaches exist, but they are informal, partial or not used consistently.
level_3: Owned reference patterns cover the common uses of AI, are applied through design review, and build in explainability, traceability and guardrails proportionate to risk.
level_4: Conformance with the patterns is checked and reported, and departures are tracked to see whether they show a pattern needs to change.
level_5: Patterns are updated from delivery experience, operating data and technology change, and retired when better approaches arrive.

title: Hosting and data location
objective: Requirements for where AI is hosted and where its data is processed and stored are defined, and each use of AI is checked against them before and during live use.
level_1: Hosting and data location are not considered; they follow whatever the supplier offers.
level_2: Location is checked for some services, usually at purchase, without stated requirements or later checks.
level_3: Documented requirements set where AI may be hosted and data processed for each class of data, and every use, including subprocessors, is checked before go-live.
level_4: Compliance with location requirements is rechecked on a set cycle and when suppliers change terms or infrastructure, and breaches are acted on.
level_5: Location requirements are refined from changes in law, risk and the market, and checks rely on continuous supplier attestation rather than one-off reviews.

title: Integration with existing systems
objective: AI is connected to core systems through supported, documented interfaces that the organisation can maintain, change and switch off.
level_1: AI is connected to other systems by whatever means works, often manual workarounds or unsupported links.
level_2: Some integrations are documented and supported, but others are informal or known only to the people who built them.
level_3: Every integration between AI and core systems is supported, documented and can be switched off safely, and AI permissions on other systems are limited and approved.
level_4: Integration health and failures are tracked, undocumented integrations are found and brought under control, and changes go through managed change.
level_5: Integration patterns are standardised and reused, and improved from incidents and change experience.

title: Managing models in live use
objective: Models, prompts and their configuration are versioned and released under control, so the organisation knows what is running and can roll back to a known good version.
level_1: Models and prompts are changed directly in live use; there is no record of what changed or when.
level_2: Some versioning exists, for example for in-house models, but prompts, settings or supplier model versions are not controlled and rollback is uncertain.
level_3: Models, prompts and configuration are versioned, released with approval and can be rolled back, with documentation for each version and advance notice of changes to users.
level_4: Releases and rollbacks are recorded and reviewed, unplanned changes including supplier model updates are detected, and failed releases are investigated.
level_5: Release and rollback are largely automated and routinely exercised, and the process is refined from release outcomes.

title: Testing and evaluation before release
objective: Before release, each AI system is tested for accuracy, robustness and behaviour against acceptance criteria agreed in advance, and released only if it meets them.
level_1: Systems are tried informally before release; there are no acceptance criteria.
level_2: Some testing is done, but criteria are set after the fact, test data is unrepresentative, or robustness and behaviour are not covered.
level_3: Every release is tested against criteria and operating conditions set in advance, on representative data, with results signed off and the approach reviewed against live performance.
level_4: Test coverage and results are reviewed across uses, releases that miss criteria are blocked or formally accepted, and test results are compared with live performance.
level_5: Test methods and criteria are refined from live performance and incidents, and evaluation is automated and repeated for every change.

title: Technology change and refresh
objective: The organisation plans for changes to models, suppliers and platforms, including suppliers withdrawing models, so that AI services continue without disruption.
level_1: Change is handled when it is forced; supplier withdrawals arrive as surprises.
level_2: Some services track supplier roadmaps or end-of-life dates, but there is no consistent planning or capacity for change.
level_3: Every AI service has a maintained, regularly reviewed bill of materials with end dates, a funded refresh plan, and recorded concentration risk.
level_4: Dependency end dates and supplier notices are tracked across the estate, changes are scheduled ahead of deadlines, and services caught by unplanned change are reviewed.
level_5: Services are designed so models and platforms can be swapped with little rework, and refresh planning is improved from experience of past changes.

title: Unapproved AI tools
objective: Use of unapproved AI tools is detected, and people using them are steered to an approved alternative or a route to get their need met.
level_1: No one knows which unapproved AI tools are in use.
level_2: Some unapproved use is known about, through reports or occasional checks, but responses are inconsistent or limited to blocking.
level_3: Unapproved AI tool use is detected by defined means across the organisation, and each finding is recorded and leads to the person being steered to an approved route.
level_4: The level of unapproved use is measured over time, repeat or high-risk use is escalated, and findings feed changes to the approved tools list.
level_5: Unapproved use is low because approved options meet need, and detection and response are refined from trends and new kinds of tool.

title: AI security baseline
objective: The organisation has adopted a recognised AI security baseline, built it into its security standards, and applies it to every use of AI.
level_1: No AI security baseline; security reviews of AI depend on the knowledge of whichever specialist is asked.
level_2: A baseline has been chosen or drafted, but it is applied only to some uses of AI or is not yet part of security standards.
level_3: An owned, recognised AI security baseline is part of security standards and applied before go-live, and every live use is monitored with logs set by risk.
level_4: Conformance with the baseline is checked and reported for each use of AI, and gaps are tracked to closure or formally accepted.
level_5: The baseline is updated from incidents, threat intelligence and changes in recognised frameworks, and the organisation contributes to shared practice.

title: AI threat modelling
objective: Each use of AI has its AI-specific threats assessed before it goes live and again when it changes, and the results shape its design and controls.
level_1: AI-specific threats are considered only when an individual raises them.
level_2: Threat modelling covers AI for some uses or teams, or uses conventional methods that miss AI-specific threats.
level_3: A defined approach covering AI-specific threats, including synthetic media impersonation, is required for every use of AI, with findings recorded and acted on.
level_4: Threat models are reviewed when uses change or new threats emerge, completion is measured, and untreated findings are escalated.
level_5: Threat modelling is refined from incidents, testing results and external threat intelligence, and common threats are handled once in shared patterns.

title: Security of the AI supply chain
objective: The security of models, data, code and services obtained from others is assessed before use and managed for as long as they are in use.
level_1: Models, data and components are taken from suppliers or public sources without a security check.
level_2: Some security checks happen, usually for large procurements, but freely available models and components are not covered.
level_3: External models, data and components are security assessed before use and reassessed over time, with security responsibilities split, documented and checked for each service from others.
level_4: Supplier security and reassessment results are measured and reported, and overdue reassessments or unmitigated vulnerabilities are escalated.
level_5: Supply chain assurance is improved from incidents and supplier performance, and the organisation shares findings with peers and suppliers.

title: Preventing information leakage through AI
objective: Sensitive information is protected from exposure through AI tools, prompts, training and outputs, with rules staff understand and technical measures that enforce them.
level_1: No specific rules; staff decide for themselves what information to put into AI tools.
level_2: Guidance exists on what not to share with AI tools, but it is not enforced and does not cover outputs or training.
level_3: Rules on which information may be used with which AI tools are communicated to staff and backed by technical measures, and tuned models inherit their data's protection.
level_4: Leakage controls are monitored, attempted exposures are detected and followed up, and results are reported.
level_5: Controls are refined from monitoring and incident data so that protection improves without adding friction for legitimate use.

title: AI in security incident response
objective: Security incident management covers incidents involving AI, with playbooks, people who have the skills to handle them, and the ability to contain an affected AI service quickly.
level_1: AI security incidents would be handled ad hoc, with no plan for AI-specific scenarios.
level_2: The incident process mentions AI, but there are no AI playbooks and few responders know how AI services work.
level_3: Security incident procedures include exercised AI playbooks, trained responders and a known containment route for each AI service, with disclosure and notification routes set.
level_4: Response performance is measured, and lessons from exercises and real incidents are acted on.
level_5: Incident response for AI is improved from exercise results, real incidents and external threat information, and lessons are shared with peers.

title: Security testing of AI before release
objective: Before release, each AI system is security tested against the threats in its threat model by suitably skilled testers, including checks that it does not disclose personal or sensitive information.
level_1: Systems are released without security testing, or with conventional checks that miss AI-specific threats.
level_2: Some security testing is done, but it is not driven by the threat model, testers lack AI skills, or safeguard bypass and information disclosure are not covered.
level_3: Every release is security tested against its threat model by suitably skilled testers, independent for higher-risk uses, including safeguard bypass for generative AI and checks for disclosure of personal or sensitive information.
level_4: Security test coverage and findings are reviewed across uses, and releases with unresolved findings are blocked or formally accepted.
level_5: Security test methods are refined from incidents and live performance, and security testing is repeated for every change.

title: AI literacy for all staff
objective: Everyone in the organisation has a baseline understanding of what AI is, what it can and cannot do, and how to use it safely under the organisation's policy.
level_1: No organisation-wide AI learning; understanding depends on individual interest.
level_2: Some AI awareness material exists, but it is optional, reaches few staff or is out of date.
level_3: Everyone who uses or operates AI for the organisation must complete a defined AI literacy baseline that is kept current, and completion is recorded.
level_4: Completion and understanding are measured across the organisation, gaps by group are followed up, and content is refreshed on a set cycle.
level_5: The baseline is updated from incidents, staff feedback and changes in AI tools, and its effect on safe use is assessed.

title: Leadership capability
objective: Leaders understand AI well enough to set direction for it, question proposals and risks, and make informed decisions about its use.
level_1: Leaders' understanding of AI depends on personal interest and vendor briefings.
level_2: Some leaders have attended AI briefings, but there is no defined expectation of what leaders should know.
level_3: Board members, executives and senior managers have completed a defined learning offer on AI opportunity, risk and governance.
level_4: Leadership capability is assessed, gaps are addressed, and the quality of AI decisions and challenge is reviewed.
level_5: Leadership learning is updated from decision reviews and external change, and leaders keep their knowledge current through ongoing exposure to AI in practice.

title: Specialist roles and careers
objective: The organisation defines the specialist AI roles it needs, with career paths and a professional community that help people grow and stay.
level_1: Specialist AI work is done by people in unrelated roles with no recognition or route to progress.
level_2: Some AI roles are defined locally, but titles, grades and expectations differ across the organisation.
level_3: Specialist AI roles are defined in the same way across the organisation, with skills expectations, career paths and an active professional community.
level_4: Progression, retention and role coverage for specialists are measured and reported, and gaps or attrition are acted on.
level_5: Roles and career paths are updated as AI work changes, and the organisation is known as a place where specialists develop.

title: Skills assessment
objective: The organisation knows which AI skills it has and which it needs, by role and group, and uses this to plan learning, recruitment and workforce decisions.
level_1: No assessment; skills are known only through individual managers' impressions.
level_2: Skills have been assessed once, or only for some groups, and the results are not used to plan.
level_3: The AI skills each role needs are defined, current skills are assessed across the organisation, and the recorded gap drives learning and recruitment plans.
level_4: Skills are reassessed on a set cycle, progress against the gap is measured, and priority gaps are tracked to closure.
level_5: Skills needs are anticipated from the AI roadmap and external change, and the assessment method is improved from experience.

title: Role-based learning
objective: People can get learning matched to what their role needs to do with AI, beyond the baseline for all staff, and use it in their work.
level_1: Learning beyond the baseline depends on individuals finding their own courses.
level_2: Some role-specific learning exists, but coverage is uneven and not linked to assessed needs.
level_3: Resourced learning pathways, linked to the skills assessment, exist for every role group that works with AI, including suppliers, and cover risk duties and AI security.
level_4: Uptake and the effect of learning on work are measured, and pathways with low uptake or effect are changed.
level_5: Pathways are updated from skills reassessment, feedback and changes in AI tools, and include learning on the job as well as formal courses.

title: Workforce planning for AI
objective: The expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills is planned for openly, with affected staff and their representatives informed and involved, and decisions made fairly.
level_1: The effect of AI on the workforce is not considered until changes are already under way.
level_2: Effects are considered for individual projects, but there is no organisation-wide view and staff learn of changes late.
level_3: Workforce plans set out the expected effect of AI on roles, numbers and skills, with options for affected staff, and are shared with staff and representatives.
level_4: Actual effects on roles and skills are tracked against the plan, fairness of outcomes across groups is checked, and differences are acted on.
level_5: Workforce planning for AI is updated from outcomes and external change, and staff help shape how roles develop.

title: Bringing in and keeping expertise
objective: The organisation recruits and keeps the AI expertise it needs and uses external experts in a way that transfers knowledge, so that capability stays when contracts end.
level_1: Expertise is hired or contracted as needs arise, with no plan for keeping knowledge.
level_2: Recruitment for AI roles happens, but retention is not managed and external engagements rarely include knowledge transfer.
level_3: A plan covers recruiting, retaining and diversifying AI expertise, and every external engagement transfers knowledge to named internal staff.
level_4: Time to hire, retention and reliance on external expertise are measured, and knowledge transfer is checked at the end of each engagement.
level_5: The balance of internal and external expertise is set deliberately from evidence and adjusted as needs change.

title: Support for staff using AI
objective: People using AI day to day can get practical help, current guidance and answers to their questions quickly from a known place.
level_1: Help depends on knowing someone who understands the tool.
level_2: Some guidance or a help channel exists for particular tools or teams, but it is hard to find or not kept current.
level_3: A known, resourced support route gives current guidance on every approved AI tool, including its limits and security risks, and tells users promptly of security changes.
level_4: Use of support, common questions and response times are measured, and recurring problems feed changes to guidance, learning or tools.
level_5: Support is shaped by how people actually use AI, and good practice from users is captured and shared back.

title: Planned approach to AI change
objective: AI adoption is managed as organisational change, with a change plan, named sponsors and the resources to carry it out.
level_1: No change approach; AI tools are made available and people are left to work out what to do with them.
level_2: Some change activity happens on individual projects, but there is no organisation-wide plan or dedicated resource.
level_3: A documented AI change plan, based on an assessment of the current culture, has named senior sponsors and funded resource, and is applied to every significant use.
level_4: Progress against the change plan is measured and reported, and areas where adoption is stalling are identified and given extra support.
level_5: The change approach is refined from what has and has not worked in earlier rollouts and from changes in the scale and type of AI being adopted.

title: Internal communication about AI
objective: Staff receive clear, honest and regular communication about what AI is being used for, why, and what it means for them.
level_1: Communication about AI is occasional, comes from enthusiasts or suppliers, and is not coordinated.
level_2: Announcements are made about some uses of AI, but they focus on benefits, are irregular or reach only some staff.
level_3: An owned communication plan delivers regular, honest messages to all staff about AI use, purpose, limits and effect on staff.
level_4: Reach and understanding are measured, for example through surveys, and messages are adjusted where staff are confused or concerned.
level_5: Communication is two-way as a matter of course, and its content and channels are improved from staff feedback and observed understanding.

title: Staff and representative engagement
objective: Staff and their representatives, including trade unions where present, are involved early in decisions about AI that affect their work, and their input is considered and answered.
level_1: Staff and representatives hear about AI after decisions are made, if at all.
level_2: Engagement happens on some projects or late in the process, often as consultation on a decided plan.
level_3: Affected staff and their representatives are involved at design stage of significant uses of AI through a defined route, their input is recorded, and they hear what changed.
level_4: The timing and effect of engagement are tracked, and uses of AI that skipped it are identified and addressed.
level_5: Staff and representatives help shape the AI agenda itself, and the engagement approach is improved from their feedback on how well it works.

title: Safe to raise concerns
objective: Anyone can raise a concern or report a problem with AI without fear of blame, and can see what was done about it.
level_1: There is no known route for raising AI concerns; problems are raised informally or not at all.
level_2: A route exists, such as a general helpdesk or whistleblowing policy, but staff do not know it covers AI or doubt that it is safe to use.
level_3: An owned, no-blame route for raising AI concerns is known to all staff, and everyone who raises a concern hears what was done.
level_4: Use of the route and staff confidence in it are measured, and response times and outcomes are monitored and reported.
level_5: Raising concerns is seen as normal practice, and the route and the response to it are improved from staff feedback and trends in what is raised.

title: Learning from what did not work
objective: Experiments and uses of AI that fail or are stopped are reviewed without blame, and the lessons are recorded and shared.
level_1: Stopped or failed work is quietly dropped; lessons stay with the people involved.
level_2: Some teams review what went wrong, but findings are not recorded or shared beyond the team.
level_3: Every stopped or failed AI experiment or use has a no-blame review, and its lessons are recorded in a shared place and passed to relevant teams.
level_4: Lessons are checked for take-up, for example in new proposals and stage gates, and repeat mistakes are identified and followed up.
level_5: Lessons from inside and outside the organisation are used routinely to shape new proposals, and stopping work early is recognised as good practice.

title: Champions and communities
objective: Networks of champions and communities of practice, with time and support to do so, spread know-how about AI and good practice across the organisation.
level_1: A few enthusiasts help colleagues on their own initiative and in their own time.
level_2: A champions network or community exists in some areas, but without agreed time, support or a link to the central AI team.
level_3: A champions network with defined roles and agreed time covers all major business areas, and a centrally supported community of practice meets regularly.
level_4: Champion coverage and activity are tracked, and the network's effect on adoption and good practice is measured and reported.
level_5: The network shapes guidance, tools and priorities, and its structure is refreshed as adoption spreads and needs change.

title: Adoption support for affected teams
objective: Teams whose work changes because of AI get practical support through the change, and actual adoption is tracked against what was planned.
level_1: Teams are given the tool and expected to adapt; nobody checks whether it is used.
level_2: Some teams get support at launch, but it stops soon after and adoption is not tracked.
level_3: Every team affected by a significant use of AI has a support plan for the change, and adoption is tracked against planned levels.
level_4: Adoption data is reviewed regularly, teams falling behind receive targeted support, and the reasons for low adoption are recorded and acted on.
level_5: Support approaches are improved from adoption patterns across many rollouts, and new rollouts plan support from that evidence.

title: Public and customer trust
objective: The organisation understands how the people it serves view its use of AI and takes that into account in its decisions and how it explains itself.
level_1: Public or customer views on the organisation's AI use are not sought; reaction is discovered only through complaints or media coverage.
level_2: Views are gathered occasionally, for example on a single project, but are not used consistently in decisions.
level_3: The views of the people the organisation serves on its AI use are gathered through a defined approach and shape design decisions and explanations.
level_4: Levels of trust are measured over time, and changes in trust or emerging concerns lead to recorded action.
level_5: The people served help shape decisions about where and how AI is used, and the approach to building trust is improved from measured results.

title: Performance measures and baselines
objective: Each use of AI has agreed performance measures and a recorded baseline of current performance before it goes live.
level_1: Measures are not set; success is judged by impression or anecdote.
level_2: Some uses of AI have measures, but they are set after go-live, lack a baseline or cover only technical performance.
level_3: Every use of AI has owned measures of accuracy, outcome, effect on people and reliance, with baselines set before go-live and proxies for risks not yet measurable.
level_4: Measures and baselines are checked at stage gates, and uses without them are stopped or held until they are in place.
level_5: Measures are refined from experience of which ones actually predicted success or problems, and common measures allow comparison across uses.

title: Monitoring live AI
objective: Live AI is monitored against its measures for accuracy, drift, misuse and unexpected behaviour, with thresholds that trigger action.
level_1: Live AI is not monitored; problems are found when users complain.
level_2: Some uses are monitored, usually for availability or cost, without checks on output quality or thresholds for action.
level_3: Every live use of AI is logged and monitored against thresholds, operating conditions, fairness measures and provider instructions, with named people to respond to breaches.
level_4: Monitoring results are reviewed on a set cycle, threshold breaches are tracked to resolution, and monitoring coverage is itself checked.
level_5: Monitoring methods and thresholds are tuned from incident history and changes in models and use, and early warning signs are acted on before thresholds are reached.

title: Benefits tracking
objective: Whether the expected benefits of AI arrive is tracked and reported, for each use and across the portfolio, and shortfalls are acted on.
level_1: Benefits are not tracked after approval.
level_2: Benefits are reviewed for some uses, usually once and informally, and not totalled across the portfolio.
level_3: A named owner tracks each use's benefits against its business case on a set schedule, and results are reported across the portfolio.
level_4: Benefit claims are checked against evidence, shortfalls trigger review of the use, and actual results are compared with forecasts.
level_5: Actual benefit data is used to calibrate new business cases and the organisation-level value case, and the tracking method is refined from experience.

title: AI incidents and near misses
objective: AI incidents and near misses that are not security incidents, such as wrong outputs, harm to people or misuse, are reported, investigated and learned from.
level_1: AI incidents are handled as they arise, if they are recognised at all; nothing is recorded.
level_2: Some AI incidents are logged in general systems, but there is no agreed definition, investigation method or record of near misses.
level_3: A defined process, linked to security incident handling, covers reporting, triage, investigation and resolution of non-security AI incidents and near misses that staff can recognise.
level_4: Incident and near miss trends are analysed and reported, and actions are tracked to completion.
level_5: Lessons from incidents, including those reported by other organisations, routinely change designs, controls and training.

title: Independent assurance reviews
objective: Uses of AI are reviewed by people independent of their delivery, with the depth and frequency of review proportionate to risk.
level_1: No independent review; delivery teams assure their own work.
level_2: Independent reviews happen for occasional high-profile uses, without a defined basis for which uses are reviewed or how.
level_3: Every use of AI gets independent review set by risk tier and triggered by change, findings are owned and reported, and AI governance as a whole is audited periodically.
level_4: Assurance coverage against the plan is reported, findings are tracked to closure, and overdue actions are escalated.
level_5: The assurance approach is refined from findings, incidents and external developments, and uses methods that test real behaviour as well as documents.

title: User feedback
objective: Feedback from people who use AI and people affected by it is gathered on a regular basis, analysed, and acted on.
level_1: Feedback is not sought; what arrives comes through general complaints.
level_2: Feedback is gathered for some uses, usually at launch, but is not analysed or acted on consistently.
level_3: Every live use of AI has a feedback route for users and affected people, with a named owner who reviews it on a set cycle and records action.
level_4: Feedback trends are measured and reported alongside performance data, and recurring issues lead to tracked changes.
level_5: Feedback is built into the service, and the way it is gathered and used is improved from evidence of what leads to useful change.

title: Re-assessing AI maturity
objective: The organisation re-runs this framework's assessment on a set cycle, compares results with earlier ones, and acts on the gaps it finds.
level_1: The assessment has been done once or not at all, and results were not acted on.
level_2: The assessment is repeated irregularly, or results are produced but not turned into an improvement plan.
level_3: A named owner re-runs the assessment on a set cycle, compares results with the previous round, and agrees an improvement plan with owners.
level_4: Progress against the improvement plan is tracked and reported, and assessment results are checked against evidence rather than self-reported alone.
level_5: Target levels and the assessment cycle are adjusted from results and external change, and results are used to set priorities across the organisation.

title: Reporting to leadership
objective: Leadership and the board receive consolidated, evidence-based reporting on AI use, performance, benefits, incidents and risk, on a set cycle.
level_1: Leadership hears about AI through occasional updates or individual project reports.
level_2: Some reporting reaches leadership, but it is not consolidated, is mostly narrative or covers only some uses of AI.
level_3: Leadership and the board receive an owned, consolidated AI report from defined data on a set cycle, with a signed assurance statement where the organisation answers upward.
level_4: The data behind the report is checked for accuracy, leadership actions are tracked, and reporting shows trends against targets.
level_5: Report content is refined from what leaders use in decisions, and the report brings in external comparison and forward-looking indicators.

title: Serious AI incidents and external notification
objective: The organisation defines serious AI incidents, can suspend a use of AI when needed, and tells suppliers, regulators and affected people through set routes and within set deadlines.
level_1: Serious AI incidents are handled case by case; nobody has decided who must be told or who can suspend a use.
level_2: Some notification duties are known, but serious incidents are not defined, deadlines are not set, or no one is named to suspend a use.
level_3: Serious AI incidents are defined, notification routes and deadlines and a decision point to suspend use are set, affected people are told under a plan, and risks short of a serious incident are reported and acted on.
level_4: Serious incidents lead to reviews of the use concerned, and notification and suspension decisions are reviewed with their actions tracked to completion.
level_5: Lessons from serious incidents, including those reported by other organisations, routinely change designs, controls and notification arrangements.
